topicName: Security (AUTH, ACLs, TLS in Transit, and RESTRICTING Commands)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Production Security Guide: AUTH, ACLs, TLS, and Command Restriction in Redis"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Securing a Redis deployment is critical because Redis is often deployed in internal networks where default configurations prioritize performance over security. By default, Redis has no authentication and allows all commands to be executed by anyone who can connect to the port."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Authentication (AUTH)"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"The simplest form of Redis security is password authentication. In modern Redis (version 6 and above), ACLs are preferred, but you can still set a global password using the requirepass directive in your redis.conf file."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"requirepass "YourStrongPasswordHere123!""},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Alternatively, you can configure authentication dynamically using the CONFIG SET command without restarting the server."},{"order":7,"type":"code","text":"CONFIG SET requirepass "YourStrongPasswordHere123!""},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Access Control Lists (ACLs)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis ACLs allow you to define granular permissions per user. You can restrict access to specific keys and commands. Below is an example of creating a restricted user who can only read keys starting with cache:."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"ACL SETUSER cache_reader on >securepassword123 ~cache:* +get"},{"order":11,"type":"bullet_point","text":"on: Enables the user account."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":">securepassword123: Sets the password for the user."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"~cache:*: Defines the key patterns the user is allowed to access."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"+get: Allows the execution of the GET command."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Encrypted Communication (TLS in Transit)"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis traffic is unencrypted by default. To prevent sniffing and man-in-the-middle attacks, you must enable Transport Layer Security (TLS). Configure the following parameters in your redis.conf file."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"port 0
tls-port 6379
tls-cert-file /etc/redis/tls/redis.crt
tls-key-file /etc/redis/tls/redis.key
tls-ca-cert-file /etc/redis/tls/ca.crt"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Restricting Dangerous Commands"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Certain Redis commands like FLUSHALL, FLUSHDB, CONFIG, and DEBUG can cause data loss or security exposure. A standard hardening practice is to rename or completely disable these commands in redis.conf."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"rename-command FLUSHALL ""
rename-command FLUSHDB ""
rename-command CONFIG "CONFIG_SECURE_TOKEN""},{"order":21,"type":"paragraph","text":"By setting a command to an empty string (" "), you completely disable it. Renaming it to an obscure string allows only administrators who know the secret token to execute it."}]
